Title: The Shift: Rethinking the Human in the Loop
Context: Despite the intention of using AI to improve efficiency and manage scale, only one-third of recruiters reported improvements in time-to-hire using AI, while 25% reported it got...
Full Text:
Ensuring that there are "humans in the loop" is the gold safety standard for making sure artificial intelligence (AI) agentic systems act safely, ethically, and legally. However, as automated processes accelerate and scale, humans lose the ability to provide meaningful oversight over machine-speed workflows. Rather than simply inserting a human into a machine process, leaders must engineer systems that enable AI agents to operate at machine speed while ensuring they act within human-authorized intent, appropriate controls, and safety and legal boundaries. This means thinking strategically about where acceleration is possible and where slowing down to human speed is necessary to avoid catastrophic risk.

The Hiring Automation “Doom Loop” Is a Warning

Hiring offers an instructive example of how humans can be sidelined by a process accelerated by unchecked automation. Machine-assisted decision-making has long been used in the hiring process to manage volume and improve fairness and efficiency. However, generative AI has made reading and writing job applications almost completely machine-dominated, leading the CEO of Greenhouse, a human resources platform, to declare that AI had created a "doom loop" in hiring. No one intended to create this doom loop, but the adoption of automation in one area led to accelerated adoption in others, ultimately sidelining humans from hiring decisions.

The hiring doom loop is driven by two mutually reinforcing trends: more applicants are applying for each position, and more companies are relying on automation to sift through the growing volume of applications. Applicants per hire tripled between 2021 and 2024, according to one survey of hiring managers, and Greenhouse reported a 412% increase in applicants per post. Applicants are almost certainly using generative AI to spin up customized applications to hundreds of jobs at once.

Meanwhile, 91% of HR departments report using AI in recruitment, and Greenhouse data shows that the number of human recruiters has dropped by over 50%. The recruiters who remain cannot meaningfully evaluate any single application at this volume, further reducing human decision-making in the hiring process. Some companies now use AI to conduct interviews, meaning applicants may not meet an actual human at the company until very late in the process, if at all.

Despite the intention of using AI to improve efficiency and manage scale, only one-third of recruiters reported improvements in time-to-hire using AI, while 25% reported it got slower. More companies are lengthening probationary periods, a sign that they're increasingly unable to identify unsuitable candidates before hiring them. Many job hunters express frustration with encountering bots instead of real humans at their potential future employer. At the same time, scammers and state-sponsored cybercriminals have taken advantage of this automated landscape to advance candidates whose real objective is to steal secrets or cryptocurrency.

A few factors made hiring one of the first processes to fall victim to the doom loop. Hiring managers were early adopters of automation, using technology like keyword-based filters to parse resumes. At the same time, successful cover letters and resumes tend to follow a formula, which makes them easy to convincingly replicate with generative AI. However, there are two factors that are not unique to hiring that make it susceptible to doom loop dynamics:

Incentives for speed and scale: as competition increases, candidates are rewarded for applying to more jobs, faster.

Mutually reinforced automation: as application volume outgrew what individuals could manage, automation spread further into the hiring process. This, in turn, drives candidates to prioritize impressing the bots rather than their future human co-workers.

The hiring doom loop is a valuable case study for managing automation because it forces leaders to account for factors outside of their direct control. Instead of responding to machine volume with more automation, developers must think strategically about the intended outcomes and potential second-order effects to ensure systems remain aligned with human intent.

Title: Prediction Markets Emerge as a New Vertical for Traffer Teams
Context: Insikt Group observed threat actors using AI to support multiple stages of their campaigns, including platform development, content creation, social engineering, and victim...
Full Text:
Executive Summary

Since the spring of 2026, Insikt Group has observed multiple Russian-language traffer teams that have quickly adapted affiliate-fraud models to capitalize on growing public interest in prediction markets such as PolyMarket and Kalshi. The platforms offered by three such teams — AtlasCore, PolyFucked, and Magnetic Team — provide websites, administrative panels, cryptocurrency payment infrastructure, victim-management capabilities, technical support, and promotional guidance. This model lowers barriers to entry for affiliates and enables campaigns to scale rapidly as new trends attract potential victims. The services combine convincing prediction-market interfaces with established fraud mechanisms designed to manipulate victims and prevent them from recovering deposited funds. These mechanisms include controlled trading outcomes, fabricated market activity, artificial withdrawal restrictions and fees, and the collection of sensitive identity and payment information.

Artificial intelligence (AI) further accelerates this opportunism by reducing the time, cost, and expertise required to adapt campaigns to emerging events. Insikt Group observed threat actors using AI to support multiple stages of their campaigns, including platform development, content creation, social engineering, and victim engagement.

The rapid adoption of prediction markets by multiple traffer teams illustrates a broader threat from mature fraud ecosystems that can pivot toward emerging technologies, financial products, and cultural trends without having to develop entirely new criminal capabilities. Prediction markets are particularly well-suited to this model because legitimate platforms already combine cryptocurrency, speculative financial activity, rapidly changing news events, and social media discussion. Fraud actors can imitate these characteristics to establish credibility and manufacture urgency. As the fraudulent prediction markets gain visibility, additional traffer teams may experiment with the prediction market theme or reuse the underlying tooling for adjacent fraud schemes.

Key Findings

AtlasCore, PolyFucked, and Magnetic Team supply affiliates with simulated prediction-market websites, administrative panels, payment infrastructure, and promotional support. Advertised compensation includes 70% to 80% of net profits for AtlasCore affiliates, a minimum 60% revenue share for PolyFucked affiliates, and a base 70% share of victim deposits for Magnetic Team affiliates.

AtlasCore’s Telegram posts recorded approximately $10.97 million in claimed deposits across its scam offerings between May 2 and September 18, 2026, with the deposits predominantly associated with prediction markets. PolyFucked separately advertises approximately $2.4 million in quarterly turnover. Both figures rely on threat actor reporting and remain unverified.

Magnetic Team advertises more than 3,000 simulated traders across more than 5,000 markets to fabricate convincing trading activity. Its code exposes configurable withdrawal-blocking pretexts, forced-loss controls, and pools of up to 20,000 deposit wallets per blockchain. AtlasCore similarly exposes settings to force wins or losses and impose individualized withdrawal restrictions.

All three traffer teams advertise or provide AI-assisted victim support. AtlasCore and PolyFucked also supply guidance for AI-generated promotional content, including synthetic influencers and branding, respectively. Magnetic Team’s source code contains indicators of likely AI-assisted development, suggesting AI use may extend to building and maintaining the underlying fraud platforms, although that assessment remains unconfirmed.

Insikt Group identified over 100 unique domains and subdomains associated with AtlasCore, PolyFucked, and Magnetic Team, including administrative infrastructure and scam websites likely operated by the teams or their affiliates.

Threat Analysis

AtlasCore

In August 2026, Insikt Group identified a post on a low-tier cybercriminal forum seeking affiliates to join the traffer team “AtlasCore”. The thread was first created on May 15, 2026, by the user “AtlasCore”. The affiliate program was also advertised on a top-tier cybercriminal forum by the user “AtlasCorp” on May 28, 2026. The program includes an offering for prediction markets, as well as more typical traffer scams such as cryptocurrency exchanges and casinos.

Title: Behind Japan’s Warnings of a Cyber Crisis
Context: The first is the breadth of the attacks: victim organizations spanned the retail, rail, logistics, media, education, and software industries, and the intrusions involved...
Full Text:
At least two features set the Q3 Japan breaches apart from other such breaches. The first is the breadth of the attacks: victim organizations spanned the retail, rail, logistics, media, education, and software industries, and the intrusions involved ransomware, stolen cloud credentials, and exploited web-facing systems. The second is the scale of the attacks: single incidents now routinely affect millions of user records or organizations downstream that rely on the targeted services, such as roughly 33 million records leaked from the EPARK PeakManager reservation platform in July and 6.6 million accounts from Times Car in September.

This trend has continued into Q4. On October 7, a ransomware incident affected IDCFrontier, a Japanese cloud provider, disrupting 495 companies and local governments. Almost a week later, on October 13, 2026, a data breach affected the Japanese software company Sourcenext. In this incident, an unidentified third party misused the company’s member information retrieval API to compromise 22,519,960 customer records containing personally identifiable information, including email addresses, passwords, names, addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth, employment information, and more.

Our observations complement October 2026 warnings issued by several Japanese agencies, including the Japan Computer Emergency Response Team Coordination Center (JPCERT/CC), the Personal Information Protection Commission (PPC), and the Innovation Platform Agency (IPA), regarding a series of cyberattacks targeting Japan-based organizations. JPCERT/CC’s notice warned of at least four consistent tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) linked to recent incidents:

Exploitation of known vulnerabilities in unpatched systems or misconfigurations;

Attacking internal and external APIs, sometimes using stolen API credentials;

Exploitation of CVE-2026-72898 (CVSS score 10), a SQL injection vulnerability, in the Metabase application;

The deployment of web shells contained within .war and .jsp files on internet-accessible web servers.

Later reports attributed the cyberattacks targeting Japanese company websites to artificial intelligence (AI) agents linked to activity ranging from basic website scanning to extended attack sequences that involved multiple tools and techniques.

Japan-based Macnica Security also reported a surge in cyberattacks since July 2026 involving personal information leaks from web systems. The company noted that this increase is unique to Japan compared with other countries. According to Macnica, of the 119 cases disclosed in 2026, approximately 68% were announced since July. This accounts for about 31% of the total 265 cases over a 34-month period. The company similarly observed unauthorized access through weak authentication, stolen credentials, or exploited software vulnerabilities and site-specific flaws in application design, APIs, or access controls. Macnica could not confirm the use of AI in these attacks.

Explaining the Increase in Incidents

Multiple factors are likely responsible for the recent increase in attacks affecting Japanese organizations.

High Demand in the Criminal Ecosystem for Japanese User Data: Criminals on the dark web place a premium on data from Japanese organizations due to Japan’s financial and identification requirements and its status as a wealthy, developed economy.

Widespread Use of Legacy Systems and Software: According to an April 2026 article by Money Forward, more than 60% of Japanese firms still use legacy systems, end-of-life software, and older operating systems. Such systems no longer receive security updates and official patches from vendors, leaving known flaws exposed to increasingly automated attempts to exploit them.

Operationalization of AI Tooling: While the specific models abused are not yet confirmed, commercial AI products are widely believed to have been leveraged in the recent spate of attacks against Japanese organizations, both for automating the attack sequence (such as automated vulnerability scanning and exploitation), and for reducing the barrier-to-entry historically attributed to the complexity of the Japanese language (such as through the easier drafting of convincing phishing emails in proper business Japanese). Notably, financial institutions in neighboring South Korea were recently the target of an intrusion campaign leveraging ARTEX, a Chinese open-source AI penetration-testing tool attributed to a group Recorded Future refers to as TAG-217. On October 19, the Japanese cybersecurity company GMO Cybersecurity by Ierae reportedly concluded that ARTEX was used in attacks against roughly 80 Japanese companies, with 8 of those attacks occurring in the 30 days prior to its report.

New Incident Reporting Requirements: Effective October 1, 2026, Japan’s new Active Cyber Defense (ACD) Law imposes mandatory reporting requirements on designated critical infrastructure operators. This is unlikely to account for the surge in reported incidents due to the law’s implementation date in Q4 2026, but it does imply that we will very likely continue to observe a higher volume of incident disclosures from Japanese organizations going forward, and the impending implementation of the law may have induced some organizations to disclose incidents in Q3 that would otherwise have gone unreported.

Recommendations

Insikt Group recommends that Japanese organizations consider the following:

Migrate away from and/or update legacy systems. Outdated and unpatched devices or software (including operating systems) provide an attractive, easy vector for threat actors to compromise organizations via previously disclosed vulnerabilities and exploits. AI-enabled scanning and automated exploitation have further increased the risk to these systems. Where possible, replace end-of-life hardware and software.

Harden internet-facing systems. Secure internet-exposed hardware and services such as virtual private network (VPN) servers, web application firewalls, load balancers, small office/home office routers, IP cameras, and DVRs by patching known vulnerabilities, restricting administrative access, enabling additional logging, and disabling unnecessary services. These devices have been increasingly exploited by cybercriminals and state-sponsored actors alike over the last several years for initial access.

Strengthen API controls. Verify authorization for every API request, test whether users can access other customers’ records, restrict API key privileges, and limit bulk data retrieval.

Protect accounts against phishing. Require phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication (MFA) and train staff to be vigilant against increasingly well-crafted Japanese-language phishing messages.

Limit data exposure and prepare for disruption. Delete unnecessary personal information, restrict data export permissions, test restoration from protected backups, and establish manual alternatives for critical services such as reservations and dispatch.

Adopt privileged access management (PAM). Limit administrative and super-user accounts, providing elevated rights only on a temporary, just-in-time basis.

Use Recorded Future Threat Intelligence. Customers can proactively monitor for threat actor mentions of their organization and leaked data on dark web forums, chat rooms, and ransomware leak sites by configuring alerts on the Recorded Future Intelligence Platform, regularly ingesting Insikt Group research, and blocklisting known malicious indicators of compromise (IoCs).

Title: TAG-217 Targets South Korean Financial Services with ARTEX
Context: The threat actor linked to recent AI-assisted attacks on South Korean financial institutions was testing infrastructure and assembling attack tools as early as August 2026,...
Full Text:
The threat actor linked to recent AI-assisted attacks on South Korean financial institutions was testing infrastructure and assembling attack tools as early as August 2026, weeks before the banking campaign became public, according to new research from Recorded Future’s Insikt Group. Subsequent public reporting indicated that the breaches exposed personal data belonging to at least 68,000 people across at least seven financial institutions.

Insikt Group’s investigation expands the known timeline and capabilities of the actor, tracked as TAG-217. Insikt Group uncovered tools designed to steal cryptocurrency wallet files, gain greater access to Linux systems, and test weaknesses in mobile devices. The findings illustrate the “jagged edge” of AI-enabled attacks: threat actors realizing significant gains while committing basic operational security mistakes. AI helps attackers pursue more targets across more environments, but does not prevent them from making the security mistakes that allowed Recorded Future to uncover preparations and capabilities beyond the reported banking campaign. Those mistakes give defenders opportunities to identify related activity and disrupt operations.

Targeting South Korean Banks

In early October 2026, South Korea’s Financial Services Commission (FSC) disclosed that multiple financial institutions had been hit by cyberattacks. The attacks had compromised different systems and allowed unauthorized access to different data at each victim entity, with one breach exposing the personal information of an outsourced developer and another resulting in the theft of customer data. Industry sources reported that the attacks involved the use of ARTEX, a Chinese-language, open-source AI penetration testing framework. The variety of targets at each financial institution likely demonstrates an advantage of AI over human operators: the ability to opportunistically test for weaknesses at scale until a valuable target is found.

On October 7, 2026, public analysis of the incident identified that the threat actor, suspected to be a Chinese speaker, used several AI tools as part of their campaign, including Claude Code, DeepSeek, Grok, and Zhipu AI. Other reports shared network infrastructure indicators used in the campaign, including a primary server running ARTEX and the use of residential proxies, likely to obfuscate the origin of the activity.

Recorded Future investigated this infrastructure to better understand the actor’s operations and tracked this activity under the designation TAG-217.

Putting Together a More Complete Timeline for TAG-217

Differentiating between agentic and human-operated attacks can be difficult, especially when skilled threat actors use AI to enhance operational effectiveness. Agentic attacks use the same tactics and techniques as human operators, though faster and at scale. In the case of TAG-217, operational security mistakes allowed Insikt Group to piece together how the threat actor used AI tools to amplify their intrusion attempts across multiple environments and to uncover earlier preparations and a broader set of capabilities than public reporting revealed.

TAG-217 routed its traffic through residential internet connections, likely to reduce the chances of detection. Recorded Future analysts used open directories within TAG-217 infrastructure to further understand its operations (Source: Recorded Future)

The culture

As we’ve grown, the office has brought together more teams, more perspectives, and more responsibilities. Futurists describe our culture in many ways, such as open, friendly, energized by positive change, and characterized by camaraderie. But, with every conversation, the same theme comes back and resonates with Boston Futurists: the sense of community. Beyond our global monthly newsletters and our fun Slack channels, we insist on making time and space to come together for in-office gatherings and celebrations.

“Even with all the change, people still show up for one another,” said Lisa Cefalo. “The office may have grown, but that sense of community has stayed with us.”

We asked longtime Boston Futurists about their favorite memories, and this is what we heard:“When a longtime team member retired — a rare event around here, so we were a little rusty at saying goodbye — everyone recorded a short video sharing what they would miss about them,” said Lisa Cefalo. “It brought her to tears, and probably a few of us, too. It was a reminder that you’re building more than a career here; along the way, you’re building a work family.”

“One of my favorite events was sailing on the Charles and hanging out with colleagues in the summer sun,” said Lacey Maddalena.

Why Recorded Future?

At Recorded Future, Futurists are given ownership of their careers and growth, backed by the resources needed to succeed and make an impact. Lacey Maddalena, a Futurist for over seven years, experienced this firsthand.

“I've been given a lot of opportunities to try new things. I started at the company as a recruiter, moved into employer branding, and now oversee our global facilities and real estate team,” she shared. “There aren't many companies that give employees the chance to try new roles and develop their careers in so many new ways.”Maura Naughton, Strategy & Business Operations Director, credits this culture of opportunities to the company’s leadership.

“I've had six different roles over the 10 years I’ve worked here,” she said. “It's been an incredible place to learn, grow, and try.”

Beyond individual professional growth, what unites team members is a clear mission: to secure our world with intelligence. Today, Futurists help secure over 1,900 clients across more than 80 countries.

“What I’ve enjoyed most is sharing the big moments with the people who made them possible,” Lisa added, reflecting on the collective impact. “We’ve navigated change and built something bigger together. Seeing how far we’ve come has been incredibly rewarding.”

Title: Russia Is Tightening Internet Controls, Leading to Operational Risks
Context: The Kremlin likely views these measures as necessary to make it more difficult for Russian elites or the public to coordinate political dissent, and for the Ukrainian government...
Full Text:
Executive Summary

Since mid-2025, the Kremlin has intensified restrictions on digital communications and infrastructure, very likely to suppress the organization of domestic political dissent and conduct digital surveillance within Russia. Increasingly strict measures targeting virtual private networks (VPNs), state-managed internet shutdowns, limitations on civilian communications platforms, and monitoring of domestic and foreign entities very likely represent an escalation from the approaches to censorship and surveillance pursued prior to 2024.

However, despite intensifying internet restrictions, technical and political limitations will likely prevent the Kremlin from achieving its long-held objective of a fully “sovereign internet” in the near term. The most likely scenario is that Moscow exerts extensive censorship and monitoring of online activity with increasingly strict –– though not absolute –– controls on circumvention and anonymizing tools.

Insikt Group assesses that the Kremlin’s primary objectives regarding internet restrictions are twofold: facilitating extensive surveillance of online activity to support control over the domestic information space while maintaining connectivity to the global internet, and developing national internet infrastructure under Kremlin control, enabling isolation from the global internet if the Kremlin so chooses. Efforts in support of these objectives have almost certainly provided the Kremlin with enhanced ability to control and monitor domestic online discourse.

In this environment, individuals and organizations operating in Russia are subject to increasing operational risks, including surveillance and exposure of sensitive data, challenges in conducting emergency communications, disruptions to corporate tools and digital applications, and legal risks. Entities with indirect exposure to Russia face an increased likelihood of supply-chain disruptions and sanctions violations and, over the longer term, face challenges in assessing the political and economic situation in Russia, as restrictions limit the availability of high-quality open sources.

Key Findings

The Kremlin is very likely using managed internet shutdowns across Russia to test and improve its ability to isolate the Russian internet, though technical and political limitations make it unlikely that it will achieve its objective of establishing a fully “sovereign internet” in the near term.

In the near- to medium-term, a combination of falling approval ratings for Russian President Vladimir Putin, declining public opinion amid economic strain, and ongoing Ukrainian drone strikes very likely incentivize Moscow to impose further internet restrictions, regardless of reported public dissatisfaction with some of these measures.

The Kremlin will very likely continue to pursue strategies to deter VPN use by forcing platforms to support VPN blocks and making VPN use more expensive and inconvenient, though likely avoiding direct punitive measures against individual users.

Kremlin Systematically Tightening Internet Restrictions

Since July 2025, the Kremlin has systematically tightened access to widely used civilian communications applications and VPNs, caused regular mobile internet outages across Russia, and instituted requirements that place Russian and foreign individuals and firms under increased government surveillance. The Kremlin likely views these measures as necessary to make it more difficult for Russian elites or the public to coordinate political dissent, and for the Ukrainian government to launch drone strikes against Russian critical infrastructure.

Restrictions Represent Marked Escalation in Control Over Russian Internet

Insikt Group assesses that, since 2012, Russians have seen their ability to operate without restriction on the internet decline in several waves, primarily driven by the Kremlin's calculation that Russians were using the internet to organize anti-government political actions.

2000–2012: Little Government Oversight

Laissez-Faire State Policy

During this period, the Kremlin generally viewed the internet as politically non-threatening, in part due to low internet penetration rates in Russia (from 1.8% in 2000 to 58% in 2011).

Thriving Media and Social Platforms

Individual expression on the internet was relatively free, with independent news sites such as Lenta, Novaya Gazeta, Ekho Moskvy, and Gazeta able to operate largely without government interference.

In addition, platforms such as LiveJournal and VKontakte (VK) –– Russia’s Facebook mirror –– operated largely without government control.

Minimal Government Regulation

Russian state telecommunications regulator Roskomnadzor was founded in 2008, but primarily handled telecommunications licensing rather than censorship or content filtering.

2012–2015: Blocklists and Platform Takeovers Following Mass Protests

Laws Passed Creating Blocklists of Websites

In 2012, following the largest protests in Russia since the fall of the Soviet Union, the Kremlin passed law No. 139-FZ, titled “On Introducing Amendments to the Law on Protection of Children from Information Harmful to Their Health and Development,” which created the Unified Register of Banned Websites. This introduced internet service provider (ISP)-level technical infrastructure, enabling the Russian government to block domains and IP addresses through domain name system (DNS) tampering.In 2014, the Kremlin passed the Lugovoy Law (No. 398-FZ), allowing for extrajudicial blocking of websites the government considered “extreme” or which called for unauthorized protests.

Platform Takeovers by the Kremlin

The Russian Government started taking over platforms it considered politically threatening. For example, VKontakte founder Pavel Durov was forced out of Russia in 2014 after refusing to hand over data to the Federal Security Service (FSB). The Kremlin facilitated the transfer of control of VK to state-aligned businessmen, including Vladimir Kiriyenko, who is currently VK's CEO.

Data Localization Targeting Foreign Internet Companies

In 2014, the Russian government passed the Data Localization Law (No. 242-FZ), mandating that foreign internet companies store Russian citizens’ personal data on physical servers inside Russia, likely to make it easier for the Kremlin to access that data for surveillance purposes.

2016–2021: Surveillance Mandates and Attempts to Block Platforms

Laws Passed to Mandate Data Sharing, Restrict VPNs, and Pursue Sovereign Internet

In 2016, the Kremlin passed the Yarovaya Law (No. 374-FZ and No. 375-FZ), which forced ISPs and communication providers to retain metadata for up to three years and message and audio content for six months, and to provide that information to Russian security services without a warrant.In 2017, the Kremlin passed the Anonymizers Law (No. 276-FZ), formally prohibiting the use of VPNs to circumvent blocked websites.In 2019, the Kremlin passed the Sovereign Internet Law (No. 90-FZ), which required Russian ISPs to install TSPU (technical means of counteracting threats, технические средства противодействия угрозам) controlled by Roskomnadzor, thereby giving the state the power to throttle or sever external traffic to a platform.

Attempts to Block Platforms Have Mixed Results

In 2018, Roskomnadzor attempted to block Telegram by IP-banning millions of cloud servers. The attempt failed, disrupting banking and retail systems without shutting down Telegram.In 2021, the Kremlin launched its first large-scale deployment of TSPU –– deep packet inspection (DPI) hardware –– to throttle a mainstream social media platform, thereby demonstrating technical maturity in the Kremlin’s ability to throttle platforms.

2022–2024: Crackdown on Independent Media, VPN Blocks

Mass Blocking and Shutdown of Independent Media

Following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the Kremlin blocked hundreds of independent news outlets (including Meduza, BBC, Radio Free Europe, and Ekho Moskvy) by pushing DNS and SNI (Server Name Indication)-level blocks to TSPU devices across all ISPs simultaneously. In addition, the Kremlin throttled, before outright blocking access to, social media platforms such as Facebook and Instagram. This was accomplished via TSPU's packet-dropping mechanism before full blocks were applied in March 2022.

In 2024, Roskomnadzor began throttling YouTube to near-unusable levels, likely to force users onto state-controlled video platforms.

Anti-VPN Actions

In 2023–2024, Roskomnadzor began blocking underlying VPN protocols, including OpenVPN, WireGuard, and Shadowsocks, via DPI hardware.

In 2024, the VPN Advertising Ban (No. 406-FZ) took effect, prohibiting the advertising of VPNs and other tools that circumvent blocks on certain websites and platforms.

Title: TAG-193’s Regional Espionage Operations
Context: Observed in April 2026 and likely used against Armenia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, this chain exploited the WinRAR vulnerability CVE-2025-8088 to place malware in the Windows...

Diplomacy, Water Security, and Resource Management

Several TAG-193 intrusions identified through Recorded Future® Network Intelligence occurred around diplomatic developments involving Kazakhstan. Following Kazakhstan’s parliamentary consideration of a treaty on allied relations with Tajikistan, we noted communications between a Tajik government entity responsible for economic development and TAG-193 infrastructure. Additionally, activity involving a Belarusian agriculture-related government entity preceded a senior bilateral meeting in Astana. While these temporal associations do not establish that the TAG-193-related activity was connected to the described developments or reveal what information the operators sought, they do provide context indicating TAG-193’s targeting interests.

TAG-193’s recurring interest in environmental and resource-management institutions is also noteworthy. Observed activity involved an Armenian government entity responsible for environmental matters and infrastructure associated with Uzbekistan’s Smart Forestry initiative, which supports digital forestry management, environmental monitoring, and ecological restoration. Additional targeting involved Nizhny Novgorod, Russia, at the confluence of the Volga and Oka rivers within the Caspian Sea basin. Although its geographic location alone does not establish a water-related collection objective, earlier reporting linked TAG-193 to the targeting of water-resource organizations across Central Asia, providing further context for this apparent interest.

In Kazakhstan, water security is closely tied to economic stability and national security. Dependence on cross-border water supplies leaves the country exposed to upstream decisions about water use, storage, and diversion. Climate change, glacier loss, and inefficient irrigation place additional pressure on water availability, with implications for agriculture, industry, and domestic supplies. The Aral Sea disaster illustrates the lasting economic, environmental, and public-health consequences of water mismanagement, helping explain why water security remains a strategic priority.

Trusted Accounts and Services Support Access

TAG-193 frequently sends spearphishing emails from compromised government accounts, using official-looking documents to make its communications credible. Identified lures included a diplomatic letter addressed to Armenia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, a Turkmenistan airspace application form, and a business proposal concerning Russia’s Orsk Oil Refinery. While not independently establishing successful compromises of the organizations these documents reference, they do indicate targeting interests.

In September 2026, Insikt Group® identified 94 high-impact vulnerabilities to prioritize for remediation, 59 of which had a Very Critical Recorded Future Risk Score. This represents a 29% increase from last month. 43 of these vulnerabilities were surfaced through the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA)’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, 37 were reported in open sources and validated by Insikt Group, and 14 were exclusively surfaced through honeypot data.

The 94 vulnerabilities identified affected products from 58 vendors, with Linux and Microsoft together accounting for approximately 13% of the vulnerabilities. The remaining exposures spanned network edge and security management appliances; operating systems (OS) and mobile devices; collaboration, content management, and enterprise platforms; artificial intelligence (AI), developer, and automation tools; and operational technology and industrial systems.

September reporting also highlighted zero-day exploitation of CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772 (NetScaler), as well as renewed exploitation of CVE-2026-35273 (PeopleSoft) against unpatched systems.

Title: Malware Indicators of Compromise (IoCs) | Recorded Future
Context: An IoC can provide the first concrete lead, while TTPs can help analysts search for related activity after an attacker changes a domain or recompiles malware
Full Text:
One malware hash can turn a vague alert into a concrete investigation. Analysts can search endpoints for the exact file, trace where it appeared, and determine whether related activity exists elsewhere. But if the attacker changes the file, the hash changes too. Domains and Internet Protocol (IP) addresses can also lose relevance as attackers rotate infrastructure.

This is why malware indicators of compromise work best as evidence within a larger investigation, not as isolated entries on a blocklist. Their value grows when analysts can establish where an indicator came from, how recently it was observed, what threats are connected to it, and whether those connections matter to their organization.

Malware indicators of compromise are technical artifacts or observations that suggest malicious activity. They help security teams detect, investigate, and contain threats, but an IoC is most useful when analysts can assess its source, timing, confidence, and relationship to other threat activity.

Key takeaways

Malware indicators can include file-based artifacts, network infrastructure, and other technical evidence associated with malicious activity.

IoCs do not exclusively describe past attacks. They can point to malicious activity that may be underway or has already occurred.

Indicator types have different defensive lifespans. An IP address may quickly lose relevance, while a file hash remains an exact identifier for the same sample even if attackers create a new version.

Threat intelligence can add context that helps analysts prioritize IoCs, connect related activity, and move from an isolated match toward a wider investigation.

What are malware indicators of compromise?

An indicator of compromise (IoC) is a technical artifact or observable that suggests malicious activity. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) defines IoCs broadly enough to include signs that an attack may be imminent, underway, or that a compromise may already have occurred.

For a security operations center (SOC) analyst or incident responder, an IoC can help answer a practical question: Have we seen evidence associated with this threat in our environment?

Analysts can use malware IoCs to validate an alert, search logs and endpoints for related activity, or scope an incident after malicious activity is confirmed. They can also use an indicator as a starting point for investigating connected infrastructure, malware, or attacker behavior.

An IoC does not automatically prove that an organization has been compromised. Context matters. Finding a malware hash executing on an endpoint carries a different meaning from finding the same hash in an intelligence feed.

IoCs and TTPs serve different purposes

Indicators of compromise identify observable evidence associated with malicious activity. Tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) describe how an adversary operates.

A specific command-and-control domain is an IoC. The techniques an attacker repeatedly uses to establish persistence or move through a network are TTPs.

Atomic indicators are often easier to match against security telemetry, but attackers may be able to change them quickly. TTP-based detection can be harder to evade when it focuses on established attacker behavior, but it can also demand richer telemetry and more detection engineering.

Security teams do not need to choose one or the other. An IoC can provide the first concrete lead, while TTPs can help analysts search for related activity after an attacker changes a domain or recompiles malware.

The most common types of malware indicators

Malware indicators generally appear either in files and host activity or in network communications. Each gives analysts a different view of what the malware has done.

File-based IoCs

File hashes such as SHA-256 fingerprints allow security tools to identify an exact known file. They provide a precise match, but attackers can alter a malware sample and generate a new hash.

Other file and host artifacts can reveal how malware operates after reaching a system. Analysts may examine suspicious file names and paths along with changes malware makes to the operating system, such as registry activity or mutex creation.

These artifacts can help investigators determine whether the same malware has appeared elsewhere in the environment.

Network-based IoCs

Network indicators show where malware connects or where malicious content is hosted.

These may include IP addresses associated with command-and-control infrastructure, domains used to distribute malware, or URLs connected to malicious activity. Analysts can also examine characteristics of network traffic when those characteristics are specific enough to the threat.

Network IoCs can help teams find infected systems that contacted known malicious infrastructure. Their usefulness can change over time because infrastructure may be abandoned, reassigned, or shared with legitimate services.

Why raw IoCs have limits

The main problem with raw malware indicators is not that they are useless. It is that the indicator alone often does not tell an analyst enough to make a good decision.

Indicators can lose defensive value quickly

Threat actors can move command-and-control infrastructure, register new domains, or change malware files to avoid known indicators. This makes some IoCs highly time-sensitive.

It is more accurate to think in terms of defensive lifespan than to assume every IoC simply expires. A hash continues to identify the same file, for example, but it stops detecting new versions once an attacker changes the sample.

A malicious label does not provide organizational context

An IP address listed as malicious does not tell a SOC whether its own systems communicated with it, whether the activity is current, or what defensive action is appropriate.

This is where raw feeds can create unnecessary analyst work. Teams must investigate why an indicator was flagged and decide whether that evidence applies to their environment.

Recorded Future recommends combining external indicator context with internal network data and subjecting indicators to organizational vetting before using them for detection in its guidance on indicators of compromise.

More indicators can create more noise

Threat intelligence feeds can contain overlapping, stale, or irrelevant information. Adding feeds without a way to assess their quality can increase alert volume without giving analysts better evidence.

Volume can still matter when a source provides useful threat coverage. It should not serve as the only measure of intelligence quality. Timeliness, confidence, provenance, and relevance also affect whether an indicator deserves attention.

IoCs do not provide complete threat visibility

Threat intelligence can tell analysts a great deal about an indicator that has already been observed. It cannot provide context for infrastructure or malware that its collection sources have never seen.

Better information about known IoCs can improve interpretation, but it does not guarantee complete threat visibility.

How threat intelligence makes malware indicators more useful

Security teams can get more value from IoCs by connecting individual observations to evidence that explains why they matter.

Recorded Future malware intelligence connects malware samples with associated IoCs and threat context. It also supports automated YARA rule generation for malware hunting.

Add context before taking action

Useful context can show when an indicator was observed, what malware is associated with it, and what other infrastructure or activity is connected to it.

Recorded Future uses Risk Scores to help analysts prioritize indicators. These scores can help determine what deserves attention, but they should inform security decisions rather than replace organizational context.

Automate repetitive IoC work

Large indicator volumes make manual lookup difficult. Application programming interfaces (APIs) and security integrations can automate IoC lookup, add threat context, and bring external intelligence into existing security workflows.

Recorded Future Cyber Operations supports these workflows through threat intelligence, APIs, and integrations.

Automation does not need to mean automatic blocking. Teams can automate research and prioritization while applying stronger requirements before an indicator triggers a direct enforcement action.

Turn individual indicators into threat-hunting leads

An IoC often becomes more useful when it leads analysts to related activity.

A malware sample can point investigators toward related variants, behaviors, and infrastructure. Recorded Future malware intelligence includes Auto YARA, which analyzes malware samples for distinctive patterns and generates YARA rules that analysts can use in malware hunting.

This lets teams move beyond searching only for a known hash and look for related files that share useful characteristics. Recorded Future University's guide to malware hunting provides more detail on how threat hunters approach that work.

Best practices for an IoC-driven security program

A useful IoC program should focus on the quality of security decisions rather than the size of the indicator database.

Check context before enforcement. Establish the source, confidence, and timing of an indicator before deciding whether it should trigger blocking or containment.

Match automation to the consequence. Automating lookup and prioritization carries less operational risk than automatically blocking infrastructure. Raise the confidence requirement as the action becomes harder to reverse.

Connect external intelligence with internal evidence. External threat data can show why an indicator deserves attention. Internal telemetry shows whether that threat has reached systems that matter to your organization.

Review active indicator sets over time. An indicator that no longer belongs in an active detection or blocking rule may still have value for historical investigation. Removing it from active enforcement does not mean deleting the intelligence.

Recorded Future's research into malware and vulnerability trends provides further context on changing malware activity and the threats defenders need to watch.

The future of IoC detection

Attackers can change hashes, IP addresses, and domains to evade known indicators. Security teams, therefore, need ways to connect individual IoCs to related malware activity and attacker behavior.

Automated malware analysis and detection-rule generation can help teams move from a new observation to a broader hunt with less manual work. This does not make atomic indicators obsolete. It gives teams another way to use them alongside behavioral detections and threat context.

FAQs about using malware IoCs in security operations

Are YARA rules the same as malware IoCs?

No. An IoC is an observable artifact or piece of evidence associated with malicious activity. A YARA rule is detection logic that searches files or other data for defined patterns. Analysts can create YARA rules from characteristics found during malware analysis, allowing them to search for related samples rather than relying on one exact file hash.

How are malware indicators of compromise collected and shared?

IoCs can come from malware analysis, incident investigations, security telemetry, threat research, and intelligence-sharing communities. Organizations can share structured threat information using standards such as Structured Threat Information Expression (STIX), while Trusted Automated Exchange of Intelligence Information (TAXII) supports the exchange of that information between systems.

Are indicators of attack the same as indicators of compromise?

No, although the distinction is not simply that one predicts an attack and the other describes the past. Indicators of attack (IoAs) focus on behaviors or activity associated with attacker intent or an attack in progress. IoCs identify technical evidence associated with malicious activity, which may relate to activity that is ongoing or has already occurred.

Can two intelligence sources assess the same IoC differently?

Yes. Intelligence sources may rely on different observations, collection methods, scoring systems, and timeframes. Infrastructure can also change ownership or use over time. Analysts should consider the source, supporting evidence, and observation dates rather than assuming every malicious classification carries the same meaning.

Title: Recorded Future Introduces AI Infrastructure Indicator Lists, Strengthening AI Governance

Full Text:
Today, Recorded Future is announcing AI Infrastructure Indicator Lists, curated datasets for security teams to identify, monitor, and implement controls for AI-related network traffic. AI Infrastructure Indicator Lists are included for free for Recorded Future customers with a Cyber Operations license.

Artificial intelligence has increasingly become enterprise infrastructure and organizations are now confronting unsanctioned tool use (also known as shadow AI), data exposure, and autonomous behavior that their controls cannot always see.

Recorded Future's AI Infrastructure Indicator Lists focus on closing this gap across risk, IT, and GRC teams whether the goal is policy enforcement, data loss prevention, or detecting shadow AI.

AI is accumulating security debt

The hidden risks of an abundance of AI within an organization are often overshadowed by the daily threats that have to be prioritized by a security team. Last year, we reported on how security debt has been accrued by almost every organization, and the unaddressed risks are piling up faster than teams can service them. As a result, blind spots in AI governance are also increasing.

Take, for example, agentic AI. Its adoption is accelerating rapidly and agents are operating across interconnected systems, giving threat actors more room to exploit vulnerabilities at the organizational level and across supply chains.

Consider a free, viral AI assistant that an employee discovers on social media and installs on their own machine to boost productivity. No procurement process, no security review, no IT visibility.

That's not a hypothetical. OpenClaw, a free open-source AI assistant, saw explosive adoption earlier this year with almost no organizational oversight. Multiply that across a workforce and security teams left trying to govern tools they don't know exist.

By 2027, an estimated 75% of employees are expected to adopt or build technology outside IT governance. As agents become more ubiquitous, defenders need to ensure they can identify which technologies are living on their networks, and begin to track and manage access permissions for autonomous processes in the same way they manage permissions for human users.

Introducing AI Infrastructure Indicator Lists

While many threat feeds give you a wall of indicators and leave you to figure out what they are and whether to trust them, Recorded Future’s AI Infrastructure Indicator Lists do the opposite.

AI Infrastructure Indicator Lists are curated, regularly refreshed datasets that map the AI infrastructure your users, developers, and adversaries are actually reaching for. Indicators include IP addresses, CIDR ranges, and domains, carrying their own Risk Scores and comment fields with service attribution.

Recorded Future provides two distinct AI-related lists: the AI infrastructure list and the Chinese AI infrastructure list. The lists cover a comprehensive range of tools, including general-purpose AI assistants, AI coding assistants, vibe-coding tools, AI search tools, voice and audio AI tools, AI video tools, Chinese-domiciled AI tools, and autonomous AI agents.
